The Recursive Flint local coding model is a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model with 40B total and 2.5B active parameters. Recursive team states that its Eureka Machine, an automated research system, helped build nearly every part of the stack. The weights are on Hugging Face under Apache 2.0. TL;DR Size: 39.8B total, about 2.5B active per token. Context: 262,144 tokens documented on the model card; the blog cites up to 512k. Runs on: 48 GB Apple Silicon Macs (M4 Pro, M5 Pro, M5 Max) or 48 GB NVIDIA GPUs. 4-bit weights take about 23 GB. Performance: Tops Recursive’s chart among MoE models under 50B on agentic coding. Trails the strongest dense models. Best: IFEval 95.1%. SWE-bench Verified 74.2%. Worst: Terminal-Bench 2.1 at 54.9%, versus 73.0% for dense Qwen 3.8. What is Recursive Flint? Flint is a decoder-only MoE Transformer for coding agents. The model investigates codebases, fixes bugs, implements features and writes tests. It is text-only and supports reasoning and OpenAI-compatible tool calls. Introducing Flint, @Recursive_SI ’s first model: a fast local coding model built with our automated research system, the Eureka Machine. • Best-in-class fast local coding • Up to 2x faster than comparable models: 125+ tokens/sec on a MacBook Pro, 150+ on RTX Spark • Built from… pic.twitter.com/ufg2xScSGw — Richard Socher (@RichardSocher) October 21, 2026 How does Flint’s architecture work? Flint has 49 layers: 2 dense layers, then 47 MoE layers. Each MoE layer has 256 routed experts. A router selects 6 per token, plus 1 always-active shared expert. Attention mixes 2 types. 35 layers use a 513-token sliding window. 14 layers use full attention with no positional encoding. There are 32 query heads and 4 key/value heads. The 2.5B active figure includes the output head. The active body alone is about 2.2B parameters. How did the Eureka Machine build Flint? The Eureka Machine proposes ideas, implements them, tests them and picks what to try next. Recursive highlights 3 contributions: Architecture: It started from a 35B-total, 3B-active baseline. It searched expert configurations and widths, landing on 40B total and 2.5B active. Quantization: It quantized the output layer (lm_head) to 4 bits, against common practice. An offline distillation stage, with the 16-bit model as teacher, recovered accuracy. This nearly halved training steps versus a quantization-aware training baseline. The NVFP4 model scores within 0.7 points of the 16-bit model. Kernels: It wrote specialized kernels for low-bit projections, MoE operations, attention and prompt processing. On M4 and M5 chips, a Metal megakernel fuses the entire decode forward pass. How does Flint perform on coding benchmarks? All scores below are self-reported by Recursive. The post IBM AI Releases Granite Speech 5.0 2B for Multilingual Transcription and Translation appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> IBM has released Granite Speech 5.0 2B , a new open speech-language model for transcription and translation. Granite Speech 5.0 2B is a 2B-parameter model from IBM that turns speech into text in 6 languages. It ships under Apache 2.0. IBM also updated 2 existing models : the edge-focused Turbo CTC and the diarization-focused 4.1 2B Plus. For developers, the release covers accurate transcription, fast on-device transcription and speaker-attributed transcripts. TL;DR Size: 2B parameters, dense. LLM backbone uses YaRN extension to 16k positions. IBM recommends audio segments of up to about 2 minutes. Runs on: GPU via Transformers or vLLM, Apple Silicon via mlx-audio, local CPU/Mac via llama.cpp GGUF (Q8_0 recommended). Performance: #2 open-weight model on the Open ASR Leaderboard, 5.68% average English WER. Best: 0.99% WER on LibriSpeech Clean. Worst: 13.79% WER on the leaderboard’s private conversational set. How does Granite Speech 5.0 2B work? The model has 3 parts, per the model card . A speech encoder of 16 Conformer blocks is trained with CTC. It uses block attention over 4-second audio blocks. A 2-layer window q-former then projects and downsamples the acoustic embeddings. Total downsampling is 10x, so the LLM sees embeddings at 10 Hz. The LLM is an intermediate checkpoint of granite-4.0-1b-base . IBM extended it to 16k positions with YaRN and fine-tuned it with LoRA adapters. Training used 390,000 hours of public audio plus synthetic data. The synthetic sets target Japanese ASR, keyword biasing and translation. Training took 40 days on 8 H100 GPUs. What is new versus Granite Speech 4.1 2B? Language ID prompting: name the input language in the prompt to steer transcription. Keyword lists up to 2,000 terms: bias output toward product names, people and acronyms. Punctuation and capitalization on request: capitalization F1 runs from 90.16 to 99.51 across test sets. Robustness: better handling of noise, reverberation and distant microphones. How does Granite Speech 5.0 2B perform on benchmarks? On the Open ASR Leaderboard , IBM’s chart shows a 5.68% average English WER. That average covers 9 public and 2 private test sets, as of October 21, 2026. Only Qwen3-ASR-1.7B scores better, at 5.40%. Note a source conflict. IBM’s blog reports 5.06% instead. That figure is unofficial, dated October 15, and averages public short-form sets only. Per-set results range widely. The model scores 0.99% on LibriSpeech Clean and 2.21% on LibriSpeech Other. It scores 13.79% on the private conversational set. On the noisy FFASR leaderboard , it ranks #4 of 42 at 14.80% average WER. Qwen3-ASR-1.7B scores 13.41% there. Multilingual CommonVoice WER is 2.60% for Portuguese and 3.50% for Spanish. Japanese is the weakest language at 10.74%. For translation, X-to-English CoVoST BLEU reaches 53.6 for Portuguese and 40.1 for German. English-to-Mandarin was not evaluated. Keyword biasing shows the clearest gain. On Earnings-22, keyword F1 rises from 67.2 to 90.1 with correct keyword lists. With 2,000-term lists mixing correct and wrong terms, it still reaches 82.8. As a Senior SE, you’ll be the technical quarterback on some of our most important opportunities: partnering with prospects and customers to design and scale their supergraph on GraphOS, and helping them prove out real impact in production.</p> <p>You’ll join a tight‑knit global SE team that collaborates closely with Sales, Marketing, Product, and Engineering—so the work you do doesn’t just close deals, it directly shapes Apollo’s roadmap and how we show up in the market.</p> <p>At its core, this role connects customer problems, Apollo’s capabilities, and value: uncovering the real problem, translating technical options into business outcomes, building technical confidence, and reducing buying risk.</p> <h2>What you’ll do</h2> <ul> <li> <p><strong>Own complex technical evaluations</strong> for strategic new and existing accounts: lead discovery, workshops, and solution design to deeply understand customer APIs, architectures, and constraints, and turn them into clear required capabilities and technical win plans.</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>Design and present multi‑system solution architectures</strong> that show how Apollo’s supergraph, GraphOS, and tooling PoCs</strong>, translating complex technical capabilities into simple, business‑aligned stories for audiences ranging from lead developers and architects to VP/C‑suite decision makers.</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>De‑risk and win complex deals</strong> by anticipating and resolving technical blockers (security, compliance, integration, performance), building customer confidence that Apollo will work in their environment, and partnering with AEs on value‑based selling, and close strategy.</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>Partner tightly with Sales, CS, Product, and Engineering</strong>: act as a trusted
